title: Biofuel Production Overview
desc: Understand how biofuels are made from crops, waste and algae, with sustainability, safety, cost and policy.
outcomes: Explain biofuel types and basic production steps.
Do simple mass and energy balances.
Write a balanced overview for a community or investor.
task: Produce a three-page overview of one biofuel pathway with process chart, balance, emissions estimate, risks and recommendation.
condition: A computer, public data, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. No production work is done.
standard: Process steps and balances are correct; emissions use stated assumptions; risks and safety are listed; sources dated; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Students, farm cooperatives, energy staff, policy assistants.
evidence: process chart, balance sheet, emissions estimate, overview
modules: Types of biofuel
Understand
Biofuels are fuels made from recently grown plant or waste material. Different types suit different engines.
Ethanol is made by fermenting sugars and blended into petrol.
Biodiesel is made from oils and fats and blended into diesel.
Biogas is made by digesting wet waste without air and burns like natural gas.
Advanced fuels use woody waste or algae and are still costly.

A bus fleet running a low biodiesel blend such as 20 per cent often needs no engine change if the engine maker allows it, while 100 per cent biodiesel may need new seals and heated tanks in cold places.
Build a table of the four types with raw material, product and use.
Table is correct and each type has one limit.
Feedstocks
Analyse
The feedstock decides cost, emissions and whether food or land is harmed.
Waste and residues such as used oil and crop stalks compete least with food.
Dedicated crops need land, water and fertiliser.
Collection and transport cost rise with distance.
Supply must be steady all year.
Used cooking oil from 200 restaurants gives about 60 litres each a month, 12,000 litres, enough for a small plant, with no new land used.
Rank three feedstocks for your place on cost, supply and land use.
Ranking is justified with one number per feedstock.
Production steps
Understand
Each pathway has stages: prepare, convert, separate and clean.
Prepare: clean, dry and size the material.
Convert: ferment, react with alcohol, or digest.
Separate: distil, wash or settle to isolate the fuel.
Test quality before sale.
In biodiesel, oil reacts with methanol and a catalyst to give fuel and glycerol. Glycerol is settled out and sold or used.
Draw a process chart for one pathway.
Chart shows inputs, steps, products and by-products in order.
Mass and energy balance
Apply
Track what goes in and what comes out to check yields.
Mass in must equal mass out including waste.
Yield = fuel output / feedstock input.
Energy ratio = energy in fuel / energy used to make it.
A ratio below 1 means the process uses more energy than it gives.
100 kg of oil plus 11 kg of alcohol gives about 96 kg of fuel and 15 kg of glycerol and loss. Yield is 96 per cent of oil input.
Complete a mass balance for 1,000 litres of fuel.
Inputs and outputs balance within 2 per cent and yield is shown.
Emissions and sustainability
Evaluate
Compare emissions over the whole life, not only at the tailpipe.
Count growing, collecting, making, moving and burning.
Compare with the fossil fuel it replaces.
Watch for land clearing, which can cancel the benefit.
Use a recognised method and state it.
A fuel from waste oil may cut life-cycle emissions by a large share, while one from cleared forest land may give no saving at all.
Estimate the saving per litre for one pathway.
Method is stated, stages are listed and the result has a range.
Safety and quality
Apply
Alcohols, gases and heat create fire and health risks; quality failures damage engines.
Alcohol vapour is flammable; ventilate and avoid sparks.
Biogas can collect and explode; install detection and venting.
Test water content, acidity and purity before sale.
Keep records of every batch.
A batch with high water content is held back, because water causes rust and microbe growth in tanks.
Write a safety and quality checklist.
Checklist has at least eight checks with limits and who signs.
Economics and policy
Evaluate
Plants live or die on cost, price and rules.
Capital cost, running cost and feedstock cost drive price.
By-products can improve income.
Blending rules and incentives vary by country.
Test the plan against a fall in the fossil fuel price.
A small plant selling fuel and glycerol earns enough only when feedstock stays under a set price per litre; the plan shows that price.
Build a simple cost per litre estimate.
Costs add up and the break-even price is shown.
Write the overview
Create
Bring the work together as a three-page document for a decision maker.
Page one: pathway, feedstock and process chart.
Page two: balance, emissions and risks.
Page three: economics and recommendation.
State what you do not know yet.
The overview recommends a waste-oil biodiesel pilot of 1,000 litres a month with a six-month review.
Write the three-page overview.
All sections are present, numbers agree across pages, and a clear recommendation ends the document.
quiz: Name three biofuels.
Ethanol, biodiesel, biogas. (Covered in module 1: Types of biofuel. To pass that module: Table is correct and each type has one limit.)
Best feedstock type?
Waste and residues. (Covered in module 2: Feedstocks. To pass that module: Ranking is justified with one number per feedstock.)
What is a co-product?
Another useful output such as glycerol. (Covered in module 3: Production steps. To pass that module: Chart shows inputs, steps, products and by-products in order.)
What is a balance?
Inputs equal outputs plus losses. (Covered in module 4: Mass and energy balance. To pass that module: Inputs and outputs balance within 2 per cent and yield is shown.)
Name an emissions source in the chain.
Land change, fertiliser, processing, transport. (Covered in module 5: Emissions and sustainability. To pass that module: Method is stated, stages are listed and the result has a range.)
Name a safety hazard.
Flammable liquids or methanol. (Covered in module 6: Safety and quality. To pass that module: Checklist has at least eight checks with limits and who signs.)
Name a quality test.
Water content, acidity, flash point. (Covered in module 6: Safety and quality. To pass that module: Checklist has at least eight checks with limits and who signs.)
Biggest cost?
Feedstock. (Covered in module 7: Economics and policy. To pass that module: Costs add up and the break-even price is shown.)
Food versus fuel question?
Avoid competing with food supply. (Covered in module 2: Feedstocks. To pass that module: Ranking is justified with one number per feedstock.)
Why check sources?
Emissions claims vary. (Covered in module 5: Emissions and sustainability. To pass that module: Method is stated, stages are listed and the result has a range.)
rubric: Yield and emission figures cite a source and unit
Figures compared across two sources, with the gap explained
Fuel standard, land use and subsidy rule for the place are written down
Rules checked on the regulator's page and the date recorded
